report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is well supported for *adults with sudden out-of-hospital cardiac arrest*: bystander hands-only (continuous chest-compression) CPR is associated with substantially better survival than receiving no bystander CPR. The causal evidence is necessarily limited—randomizing people to “no CPR” would be unethical—but the consistent observational evidence, physiology, and guideline recommendations support acting immediately.

A large nationwide Japanese observational study compared compression-only CPR, conventional CPR (compressions plus breaths), and no bystander CPR. It found both CPR approaches improved one-month survival with favorable neurologic outcome versus no bystander CPR, particularly when the arrest was presumed cardiac and CPR began quickly.  
https://www.bmj.com/content/342/bmj.c7106

The AHA summarizes the broader evidence as showing that immediate CPR can double or triple survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, and states hands-only CPR is as effective as CPR with breaths during the first few minutes of an adult sudden cardiac arrest.  
https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats/  
https://cpr.heart.org/-/media/cpr-files/courses-and-kits/hands-only-cpr/handsonly-cpr-faqs-ucm_494175.pdf

**Important qualification:** “Hands-only” is not universally interchangeable with conventional CPR. Evidence reviews find no clear overall difference between compression-only and conventional CPR, rather than proving hands-only is superior. Rescue breaths remain especially important for children, drowning, overdose/respiratory arrest, and prolonged collapse.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34622436/

For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, call emergency services, obtain an AED, and start hard, fast chest compressions; doing hands-only CPR is far preferable to doing nothing.
